schools.summary: Gill identifies the speaker as Jehovah the Son of God, the eternal Word, very probably appearing in a human form since an object was seen as well as a voice heard, and explains the storm as raised to give notice of the appearing and to command reverence; he notes that Elihu had seen it rising and hastened to finish, and that one Targum calls it the whirlwind of distress, answering to Job's own condition.

Henry makes the speaker the second person of the Trinity, by whom the worlds were made and who afterwards spoke from Sinai, beginning here with the creation as there with the redemption out of Egypt; and he explains the timing, that when all had had their say without gaining their point it was time for God to interpose, convincing Job of his unadvised speaking and then convincing the three friends that they had wronged him.

Wesley describes the dark and thick cloud out of which a tempestuous wind was sent as the harbinger of the presence. Clarke works on the Hebrew and finds a different word from the one used a chapter earlier, meaning something turbulent and violently agitated, and reports that the Chaldee renders it a whirlwind of grief, which makes the scene allegorical rather than real.

Ellicott reads the chapter as the grand climax and catastrophe of the poem, since nothing but darkness could remain unless he whose government was in dispute intervened, and states the single argument the remaining chapters develop, that man's ignorance of nature makes it absurd for him to judge God's moral government; he notes that although Job is justified later, the tone here is mingled with reproach.

debates.question: Why does the answer come at this point?
debates.positions: Henry explains it by the exhaustion of the human speakers, each having silenced another without convincing him; Ellicott explains it structurally, as the only possible resolution of a dispute about God's own government.

outliers.view: Notes that the word for the storm is not the one used in the previous chapter, and that the Chaldee's whirlwind of grief turns the whole scene into something impressed on Job's imagination rather than seen.

themes: the Lord answered Job
out of the whirlwind

schools.summary: Gill denies that the question is addressed to Elihu, as some have thought, since it was Job the Lord answered and Job who took the words to himself, and explains that God asks not as ignorant but as wondering that such a man should talk so; on the summons he has Job girded like a man of valour putting on his harness for battle, the allusion being to the long eastern garments gathered up for work or war, and observes that Job had blustered what he would do and is now dared to do it.

Keil and Delitzsch argue from the participle that Job must have uttered such words immediately before and been interrupted by Jehovah without any intervening speaker, and notice that the word for counsel deliberately stands without the possessive. Ellicott answers the question from Job's own earlier words, that this is a dying and enfeebled man, not even in his best estate but persecuted and exhausted, and so altogether unequal to the task he has undertaken.

Clarke paraphrases the question as a challenge to one who pretends to speak on the deep things of God and leaves his counsels the darker for the explanation, and hears reassurance as well as challenge in the summons, since the questions to come are easier than those Job presumed to discuss; he adds that the most convincing manner of arguing is by interrogation. Wesley marks the effect rather than the sense, that this first word struck Job to the heart and is echoed back by him at the end as the arrow that stuck fast in him.

Gregory asks why the rebuke was needed at all, and answers that since Job was to be restored rather than called out of the world, God was obliged in strict justice to reprove the man he preserved alive, lest his very victory lay him low with the sword of pride; nothing slays a soul more fatally than the consciousness of virtue, which puffs it up and diverts it from the intention of improvement.

outliers.view: Holds that Job was just before his scourges and more just after them, raised the higher in the praise of God as he was smitten with the heavier chastisement.

themes: who is this that darkeneth counsel
by words without knowledge
gird up now thy loins like a man

schools.summary: Clarke paraphrases the opening question bluntly, that Job has a limited and derived being and is only of yesterday, and on the measures reaches for the physics, asking who adjusted the polar and equatorial distances from the centre, who formed the zones and great circles, and who fitted the magnitude and gravity of the whole to its orbit; on the singers he holds that the words must refer to intelligent beings existing before the visible heavens, takes both clauses for the angelic host, and notes that the Chaldee renders it all the troops of angels. Wesley puts the first question in a sentence and explains both titles of the singers, morning stars for their lustre and sons of God because they had their whole being from him.

Henry turns the question into a pair of propositions, the greatness of God who laid the foundations and the meanness of a man not so much as present, and observes that we had no hand in the making of the world and so nothing in it entitles us to a dominion over it.

Gill puts Job in a state of nothingness when the work was done, notes the oddity in the figure, that the earth has foundations so firm it cannot be moved and yet hangs upon nothing, and then turns the question on the learned, since mathematicians pretend to give us the circumference and diameter of the earth but are not agreed and widely differ; he alone keeps the literal sense of the morning stars open, since all stars may be so called, while adding the figurative readings of angels, of ministers, and of Christ as the principal morning star.

Ellicott reads the architectural comparison as a concession to the feebleness of man, one that itself heightens the effect of the answer the question compels, and takes the singers for the angels entrusted with the guardianship of the stars, remarking that Milton borrowed his conceptions from the verse.

debates.question: What sang at the founding of the earth?
debates.positions: Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all take both clauses of the verse for the angelic host; Gill keeps the literal sense of stars open alongside the figurative readings of angels, of ministers of the word, and of Christ himself as the principal morning star.

outliers.view: Draws the inference Job is meant to feel, that the heavenly witnesses neither advised nor assisted in the work, nor censured any part of it, as Job had presumed to do.

themes: where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth
who laid the corner stone thereof
when the morning stars sang together

schools.summary: Gill marks the transition as following the order of creation, from the earth to the sea, and insists the verses describe not the flood, as some interpret them, but the first creation, the sea represented throughout as an infant, here still in embryo and shut up in the bowels of the earth as a child in its mother's womb.

Clarke calls it a very fine metaphor, the sea issuing from the womb of the void and formless chaos, and presses the detail of the clothing, the cloud answering to the cloth in which a new-born infant is received and the thick darkness to the swathing that supports a body too tender for careful handling; he adds an allusion to the opening of Genesis, where darkness lies on the face of the deep. Wesley takes the rising vapours as the garment and the black clouds as the bands, then withdraws the figure to make his point, that neither clouds nor air nor sands nor shores can bound the sea, but God alone.

Keil and Delitzsch set the scene in the order of the primeval states, the formless void being the first half and the deep the second half of the earth's early condition, and note that the question passes over the intermediate stage in which the waters of sky and earth were not yet separated.

outliers.view: Uses the image and then takes it back, since nothing physical actually bounds the sea: not clouds, not air, not sands, not shores, but God alone.

themes: who shut up the sea with doors
as if it had issued out of the womb
the cloud the garment thereof

schools.summary: Gill renders the clause with an older English translator as breaking the earth by decree, a vast chasm made to hold the waters, God cleaving the ground and raising the hills and sinking the valleys so that channels were formed, and refers this to the work of the second day; on the word that halts the waves he keeps to the coasts and the tides, the sea spreading to such and such shores and no further and its tides running up the rivers and returning, keeping exactly to time and place.

Wesley describes the hollow places as a cradle to receive and hold so great an infant, with bounds fixed as strongly as if fortified with bars and doors. Clarke traces the decree to the command in Genesis and identifies the bars and doors with the geography itself, the dry land forming the barrier and the great rivers and bays the doors; he then answers the same question mechanically, tracing the limitation of the tides to the attraction of the sun and moon, to gravitation toward the earth's centre, and above all to the rotation that carries any point out from under the direct attractive influence before the waters can rise to any extraordinary height.

Ellicott prefers a different rendering, that God prescribed for it his decree rather than broke up a place, and adds the reflection the verse invites, that given the vast forces and unstable nature of the sea it is a marvel it acknowledges any limits at all.

debates.question: What does the clause about the decreed place mean?
debates.positions: Gill and Wesley take it of a physical breaking of the ground to form the sea's bed; Ellicott renders it instead as prescribing a decree, that is, determining the boundaries of its abode.

outliers.view: Answers the poetry with mechanics, finding the bars and doors that stay the proud waves in lunar and solar attraction, in the earth's gravitation toward its own centre, and in the rotation that keeps any part of the surface from lying long under the direct pull.

themes: brake up for it my decreed place
set bars and doors
hitherto shalt thou come, but no further

schools.summary: Gill observes that Job had lived to see many a morning but it never was in his power to command one, and had sometimes wished for the light before its time without being able to hasten it; of the morning's reach he has the light take hold of the extremities of the hemisphere as soon as it springs, and applies the image to the spread of the Gospel to the ends of the earth.

Wesley reads the challenge as covering the whole order, whether Job created the sun and appointed the succession of day and night, and explains the effect on the wicked by two causes, that the light discovers them where darkness hid them and that morning was the usual time for executing judgment. Clarke refers the first clause to the dawn, the twilight produced by refraction in the atmosphere, by which the light reaches us gradually instead of bursting at once on eyes it would injure, and the second to the annual revolution, since the sun does not rise in the same point of the horizon on two successive days in the whole year; he also makes the picture concrete, the thieves and assassins and adulterers who hate the light flying like ferocious beasts to their dens as soon as it dawns.

Henry makes the light the first of six things Job is challenged to account for and turns its familiarity into the argument: there is no visible being of which we are more firmly assured and none we are more puzzled to describe, and the day-spring knew its place before we knew ours, for we are but of yesterday.
Ellicott glosses the dayspring's place as changing from day to day with the changing seasons, and identifies the figure of the wicked being shaken out as that of a man shaking a cloth.

outliers.view: Proposes a rearrangement of the text, holding that the verse about the light withheld from the wicked connects immediately with this one and that the verse about the seal disturbs the connection.

themes: hast thou commanded the morning since thy days
caused the dayspring to know his place
that the wicked might be shaken out of it

schools.summary: Gill takes the clay for the earth itself, shapeless in the dark like the chaos at the beginning and receiving a form under the light as clay receives the impress of a seal, and adds the spiritual application he finds throughout the passage, the change the light of the Gospel makes in men; on the last clause he explains the light withheld from the wicked as the loss of what they counted light, since their day is the night, and allows two figurative senses besides, the light of prosperity removed and the light of life extinguished.

Wesley distinguishes what it is that stands forth under the light, the natural things such as living creatures, herbs and trees, and the artificial, such as houses and other buildings, and divides the withholding between two causes, the wicked's own choice of darkness and the judgement of God or of the magistrate by which they are cut off from the light of the living; he glosses the broken arm as the strength they had used in oppressing others. Clarke reads the clay instead as the earth's capacity to modify itself into endless forms, pointing to the variety of plants and flowers as proof, and adds an antiquarian note on the Eastern brass seals for stamping pottery, six of which lay on his own desk with fine clay still in their perforations.

Ellicott renders the verse that the earth is changed as clay under the seal and all things stand forth as in their proper raiment, every object being without form in the darkness as clay or wax is until the seal is applied.

debates.question: What is the clay that the seal stamps?
debates.positions: Gill, Wesley and Ellicott all take it for the earth, formless in the dark and given shape by the light; Clarke takes it for the earth's own plasticity, the endless forms of its vegetable productions, and reports another translator who applies the whole verse to the rays of light rather than to the ground.

outliers.view: Reports a rendering on which what is broken off is the roving of wickedness, the wicked being no longer able to pursue their predatory excursions.

themes: it is turned as clay to the seal
they stand as a garment
from the wicked their light is withholden

schools.summary: Gill offers a range of renderings for the springs of the sea, the subterranean passages that supply it, the fountains rising at its bottom, the drops nobody can count, its perplexities or thickets, its rocks and shelves, or its borders; on the gates of death he specifies that the ones meant are those by which men pass into the state of the dead, and lists what is hidden, since we know neither what death is nor in what way or at what time we shall go out of the world, there being no correspondence between the dead and the living; and on the breadth of the earth he answers that a man who lived as long as Methuselah could never survey it all.

Wesley keeps the Hebrew figure that the word is tears, the springs out of which the waters flow as tears do from the eyes, and writes at length on death as a grand secret, that we cannot describe how the knot is untied between soul and body, and that while we are here in a world of sense we speak of the world of spirits as blind men do of colours. Clarke admits the limit plainly, that of these springs we know just as much as Job did, reports the old opinion that fresh matter oozed in through a porous bottom with the obvious objection that it might as well ooze out, and presses a logical difficulty on the second verse, that death cannot be called the privation of life, for what then would the shadow of that privation be?

Ellicott prefers the mazes and intricacies of a trackless deep and notes that this leads naturally to the cognate thought of the bottomless pit of death; on the breadth of the earth he observes that the language belongs to an older picture of the world, a vast plain, and adds that although all this language is unscientific its majestic sublimity is not one whit affected thereby.

debates.question: What are the springs of the sea?
debates.positions: Gill canvasses subterranean passages, fountains on the sea floor, drops, thickets, rocks and borders without deciding; Wesley keeps the Hebrew word for tears; Ellicott prefers the mazes of a pathless deep; Clarke reports and dismisses the philosophers' porous bottom.

outliers.view: Distinguishes the two terms of the verse, death and the shadow of death, taking the second for the intermediate state, the openings into the place of separate spirits.

themes: the springs of the sea
the gates of death
hast thou perceived the breadth of the earth

schools.summary: Gill glosses the question narrowly as the way to the place where light dwells, applies the following verse chiefly to the light, taken as it were by the hand and guided to its utmost bound, and answers the closing verse as a plain question, replying that Job was not born when light and darkness were first separated and that even the first man could not have been present, since man was not made until the sixth day.

Clarke turns the first question into a challenge to natural philosophy, asking what light is, since it is not in the sun and was before the sun, and whether it is philosophical to call darkness the mere privation of light; he observes that darkness and light are here personified as real intelligent beings with local dwellings and defends the liberty, since poetry animates everything. Wesley asks the same in an older idiom, where the sun goes when it departs from this hemisphere and whence light came into the world when nothing but gross darkness was upon its face.
Ellicott glosses the verb of the second verse as going with or tracking the light, and holds that the closing verse is better read without an interrogation, as sublime irony.

debates.question: Is the closing verse a question or an irony?
debates.positions: Clarke calls it a strong and biting irony which a literal rendering proves, and Ellicott would print it without an interrogation mark; Gill answers it straightforwardly as a question, on the ground that Job was not yet born.

outliers.view: States what he takes the irony to be for: Job had valued himself too much on his knowledge, and a chief object of the speech is to humble that knowing pride.

themes: where is the way where light dwelleth
the paths to the house thereof
knowest thou it, because thou wast then born

schools.summary: Gill identifies the treasuries with the vapours and clouds of the atmosphere and gives three reasons for the word treasure, that they are hidden until they fall, that they are at the command of their proprietor, and that they are enriching, since snow lying on the earth keeps it warm; he then guards the image against being pressed, warning that we are not to imagine heaps laid up in times past against times to come. On the parting of the light he offers several possibilities, the first division of light from darkness, the daily separation at sunrise and sunset, the two hemispheres, the poles with their six months of each, or the darkness over Egypt with light in Goshen, and objects to the reading that takes the verse of lightning, since lightning is mentioned later.

Wesley keeps the plain question, whether Job knows where those vast quantities are laid up, and explains the second clause of the parted light by the old notion that the sun is the father of the winds. Clarke prefers to ask how snow and hail are made, describes hail as composed of many small spherules frozen together rather than a single drop, traces both to electricity and admits candidly that the theory is not in all cases supported by the facts; he takes the parted light of lightning after all, and turns it into a catalogue of what electrical science had not settled, from its velocity to the cause of its zigzag form.
Ellicott names the hailstorm that fell on the Canaanite kings as the day of battle meant, and glosses the parting of the light as its distribution in turn to all the inhabitants of the earth.

debates.question: Is the parted light daylight or lightning?
debates.positions: Gill takes it of daylight and objects that lightning is mentioned in a later verse, and Wesley and Ellicott read it the same way; Clarke takes it of lightning and builds his whole note on the difficulty of describing how the flash divides.

outliers.view: Gives the first phrase a different sense, the season of strictness, when the earth is bound by the frost, rather than a time of trouble.

themes: the treasures of the snow
against the day of battle and war
by what way is the light parted

schools.summary: Gill rules out an aqueduct of the kind men cut from the Nile and puts the channel in the atmosphere, a course for the rain to come down by, steered so that it falls gently rather than in spouts and floods and on whatever part of the earth God pleases; on the wilderness he notes that there is nobody there to cultivate it and nobody to profit by the rain, and yet the Lord sends it for the animals that dwell there, and he reads the desolate ground as an emblem of the Gentile world satisfied at last by the rain of the Gospel.

Wesley says that without this providence the showers would fall confusedly and overwhelm the earth, and asks who opened a passage for the lightning and thunder out of the cloud in which they were imprisoned. Clarke derives the word from a root meaning to ascend, so that it may mean a cloud, since he cannot see how a torrent can ascend except by evaporation, and notes that by that contrivance the earth is not only watered but dried; on the thunderbolt he has God launching it and making the road it runs in, and observes that heathenism reserved that act to its supreme god.
Ellicott corrects the rendering to a channel cleft for the water-flood, and puts the conclusion of the passage in a line, that God is mindful of his creation independently of the wants of man.

Henry marks the turn of the whole speech here, that the questions have hitherto been fitted to convince Job of his ignorance and now, in the same manner, are to show his impotence, since it is as little that he can do as that he knows; and he adds that nothing is more uncertain than what weather it shall be, or further out of our reach to appoint.

debates.question: Is the watercourse cut in the ground or in the air?
debates.positions: Gill, Wesley and Ellicott all place it in the atmosphere, a channel by which the rain descends in order; Clarke derives the word from a root meaning to ascend and suggests it names the cloud itself, where the waters are stored, or possibly a waterspout.

outliers.view: Reaches the same conclusion by meteorology rather than by providence: the thunder cloud is conducted over deserts as well as over inhabited countries so that the tender herb may spring for the beasts and insects that live there.

themes: who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters
to cause it to rain on the earth, where no man is
to satisfy the desolate and waste ground

schools.summary: Gill says the rain has no father but God and notes that the heathens themselves gave their supreme god a title of that kind, taking the same for a figure of the Gospel, which is not of men but comes down from heaven; he calls God the parent of ice as of rain and dew, observes that Scripture elsewhere calls it his ice, and remarks that the verse represents the Lord as a mother, a way of speaking he finds in an ancient poet who joined both parents in one name. Of the frozen surface he says it will bear great burdens and let carriages pass where ships went before, and turns it into an emblem of the hard heart of man, which only the power and grace of God can thaw.

Wesley reduces the first question to a single line, whether any man can beget or produce rain at his pleasure. Clarke turns to the dew, quotes a definition of it as a thin insensible mist descending while the sun is below the horizon, and reports an unsettled controversy, since experiments made to determine whether dew rises from the earth or descends from the air had alternately favoured each; on ice he lays out the theory current in his day that ice is really the natural state of water, explains why it floats by the air-bubbles produced in freezing, and notes their expansive power, sufficient to burst the strongest vessel.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the parallelism asks after a begetter in the one line and a bearer in the other, so that rain and dew have no created father as ice and hoar-frost have no created mother. Ellicott renders the last verse that the waters hide themselves and become like stone, losing their familiar quality altogether.

outliers.view: Leaves the origin of dew an open question, since the experiments pro and con have alternately preponderated and we can no more tell than Job whether it rises from the ground or is deposited from the air.

themes: hath the rain a father
out of whose womb came the ice
the waters are hid as with a stone

schools.summary: Wesley states the contrast most plainly, that the one cluster brings in the spring and the other rises in November and brings in winter, so that both seasons will have their course; God can change them when he pleases, making the spring cold and the winter warm, but we cannot. Clarke gives the astronomy, six stars visible to the naked eye and seven to a good eye on a clear night though a telescope shows ten times that number, passes on another writer's judgement that the winter constellation stands by an elegant figure for winter at large, and reports a quite different derivation for the next name, from a root meaning to corrupt, on which it would be the pestilential summer wind of Arabia rather than a constellation; on the ordinances of heaven he turns the question on his own century, since Newton's system is most probably the true one and yet gravity is essential to it and Newton could neither explain nor comprehend what gravity is.

Gill takes the first phrase as the pleasantnesses of the season, which cannot be hindered from taking place in the proper course of the year, reports the alternative rendering of bands on which the question becomes whether Job could bind such a group together, and applies the whole to the irresistible influences of grace; he identifies the next name with the chambers of the south, the southern pole and its stars hidden from sight in this part of the globe, while noting that some take it for the zodiac, and describes the ordinances as laws so far from being made by men that they are not even fully known by them.

Ellicott weighs the two senses of the first phrase, influence or band, and thinks the parallel with the bands of the other constellation favours the second; he takes the zodiac reading of the next name as the common one and identifies the children of the northern constellation with the three stars in the tail of the Bear.

debates.question: What does the first phrase of the verse mean?
debates.positions: Gill and Wesley take it of the sweet influences of the season, which cannot be restrained; Ellicott and the versions Gill reports render it instead as bands or twistings, so that the question is whether Job could cluster such stars together.

outliers.view: Enters a caution about all these identifications, that other scholars find them certain where he is obliged to doubt, and that he is reluctant to depart from the ancient versions but dares not follow where he cannot see the groundwork.

themes: the sweet influences of Pleiades
the bands of Orion
canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season
the ordinances of heaven

schools.summary: Clarke puts the contrast of voices exactly, that thunder is called voices in the Hebrew because it is reckoned the voice of God, so that Job's voice is here set against the voice of Jehovah; he notes that the heathen made their chief god the holder of the forked lightning, grasping the flame so that it cannot escape however it struggles, and remarks that the Hebrew word for lightnings carries both the sense and the sound of thunder. On wisdom in the inward parts he keeps the human sense and turns it into a reflection on the limits of thought, that the deepest contemplation cannot investigate truth without the inspiration of the Almighty and that a man who knows nothing of his own mind can hardly comprehend an infinite Spirit.

Gill draws the practical distinction the verse implies, that Job may call to the clouds as long as he likes and not a drop will be let down, because rain is to be had in a suppliant way through the prayer of faith and not in a dictatorial one; and he presses what it would mean if the lightnings were at the call of men, since Elijah called down fire under the impulse of prophecy and not for imitation, and the disciples were severely reproved for wanting the same on a provocation.

Ellicott confesses that the mention of the inward parts and the heart in the middle of natural phenomena perplexes everyone, and proposes referring them to the lightnings just personified, so that the question asks who put such understanding into them.

debates.question: Whose inward parts are meant?
debates.positions: Gill and Clarke both take the verse of man, and read it as continuing the argument from human incapacity; Ellicott, finding the placement inexplicable, refers it to the lightnings of the previous verse, and Clarke reports the same alternative without adopting it.

outliers.view: Argues from the consequences: if lightnings were at the disposal of men, dreadful things would be done, since if good men when provoked would use such a power to destroy life, how much more bad men.

themes: canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds
canst thou send lightnings, that they may go
who hath put wisdom in the inward parts

schools.summary: Gill allows two senses for numbering the clouds, counting them when the heavens are full or declaring their matter and motion and use, neither of which any man can do completely, and reports a Jewish reading on which the question is who can make the sky clear as sapphire when it is overcast; he reads the hardened ground as dust attenuated into powder while the clods cleave together as if glued, which happens in a drought for want of rain, though he allows the opposite case of the bottles being poured out.

Clarke suggests that the verb may bear an Arabic sense and mean to irradiate, referring to the inimitable tinges sometimes seen in the sky, and explains the bottles of heaven as an allusion to the skin bottles in which water was carried from wells; he reads the hardening as a question about the cohesion of matter itself and answers it with a chemist's catalogue, asking how measured parts of alumine and silex and oxide of iron make a ruby or an emerald, and noting that even water in a solid form enters into several gems as their water of crystallization.

Ellicott notes that the second clause is understood in two opposite senses, of pouring the bottles out or of laying them up in store, and that the choice is hard because the following clause is itself uncertain, according as the hardened ground is taken for thick mud or for dry soil; with this verse, he observes, the survey of physical phenomena ends.

debates.question: Are the bottles of heaven poured out or stored up?
debates.positions: Ellicott reports both senses and declines to decide, since the following clause about the hardened ground is itself ambiguous between mud and drought; Gill reads the ground as parched for want of rain while allowing the opposite case.

outliers.view: Turns the question about hardening into one about the principle of cohesion in matter, which he does not think anyone can solve.

themes: who can number the clouds in wisdom
the bottles of heaven
when the dust groweth into hardness

schools.summary: Gill marks the turn from meteors to beasts and birds and reports that some begin the next chapter here; he calls the lion the strongest and fiercest of beasts and answers that man neither can hunt for him nor would dare to if he could, passing on two things from the naturalists, that a small creature between a fox and a wolf goes before the lion and hunts for him, and that young lions hunt for the old ones when these can no longer go in search themselves. He reports the reading that makes the couching lions old ones waiting for whatever passes, objects that the same coverts serve the younger, and takes the picture for an emblem of cruel persecutors and bloodthirsty tyrants.

Clarke holds that the best Hebrew Bibles begin the new chapter with this verse and begin it properly, prefers to render the word of the lioness, and turns the question on Job's own equipment, since he has neither the animal's strength nor its instinct nor its cunning; he refers the couching to the young, who lie under cover to surprise what they are not fleet enough to overtake, and derives the Hebrew name for a whelp from a root meaning to cover or hide. Of the raven he thinks the bird was chosen for its appetite and its continual cry, which is the cry of hunger, and because it dares not frequent the dwellings of men, being reckoned a bird of ill omen. Wesley states the contrast the chapter ends on, that having named the noblest of the brute creatures God now names one of the most contemptible, and draws the inference that he who provides for the young ravens will not fail to provide for his own children.

Ellicott agrees that the new chapter ought to begin at the lion, since the animal creation now passes under review, and corrects the grammar of the last clause, which is not a separate statement but dependent on what precedes, so that the wandering for lack of meat belongs with the crying.

debates.question: Which lions are meant by those that couch in their dens?
debates.positions: Clarke refers the couching to the young, too slow as yet to run their prey down and named from a root meaning to hide; Gill reports the reading that makes them old lions lying still for want of strength, and objects that the same coverts serve both.

outliers.view: Quotes a poet's paraphrase of the verse and the note attached to it, that the raven is named as the care of Providence because her clamorous voice seems always to be calling upon it, and that the noisier ravens of the Nile are probably the ones meant.

themes: wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion
when they couch in their dens
who provideth for the raven his food
